items.question: How many seats does the H135 T3 have in the basic version, and what is the maximum optional seating arrangement, per Sect. 7.1.1?
options: Five seats basic version, optional arrangements for up to eight persons
Four seats basic version, optional arrangements for up to six persons
Six seats basic version, no optional arrangements
Eight seats basic version, optional arrangements for up to ten persons
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1 describes the EC135/H135 T3H as a light twin-engined multi-purpose helicopter with five seats in the basic version and optional seat arrangements for up to eight persons; the pilot's seat is on the RH side.

items.question: What engine control system enhances the reliability of the H135 T3's two Turbomeca ARRIUS 2B2 engines, per Sect. 7.1.1?
options: Digital engine control (FADEC) system
Manual mixture control only
Analog fuel governor without digital control
A single shared engine control unit for both engines
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1 states the EC135/H135 T3H is powered by two Turbomeca ARRIUS 2B2 engines with digital engine control (FADEC) system, with reliability further enhanced by a fully-separated fuel system, dual hydraulic system, dual electrical system, and redundant main transmission lubrication.

items.question: What type of main rotor is the H135 T3 equipped with, per Sect. 7.1.1?
options: A four-bladed bearingless main rotor (BMR), with blade pitch controlled through integrated glass/carbon fibre control cuffs
A two-bladed teetering rotor system
A five-bladed fully articulated rotor system
A three-bladed semi-rigid rotor system
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1 states the helicopter is equipped with a four-bladed bearingless main rotor (BMR); the inboard flexbeam enables blade movement in all axes, with blade pitch angles controlled through integrated glass/carbon fibre control cuffs.

items.question: What type of antitorque system does the H135 T3 use, and how many tail rotor blades does it have, per Sect. 7.1.1?
options: A "Fenestron-type" antitorque system with a 10-bladed tail rotor
A conventional exposed two-bladed tail rotor
A NOTAR (no tail rotor) system
A Fenestron system with 4 blades
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1 states the helicopter is equipped with a "Fenestron-type" antitorque system, having a tail rotor with 10 blades, controlled via a "Flexball" type cable routed from the pedals to the Fenestron's input control lever.

items.question: What redundancy design does the main rotor hydraulic control system have, per Sect. 7.1.1?
options: A duplex system with tandem piston (both systems active); if one system fails, the remaining system has sufficient power for safe flight and landing
A single hydraulic system with a mechanical backup only
No hydraulic assistance is used for main rotor controls
Triple-redundant hydraulic systems, all three active simultaneously
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1 states the hydraulic system for the main rotor controls is designed as a duplex system with tandem piston, with both systems active; in case of a failure of one system, the remaining system has sufficient power to ensure safe flight operation and a safe landing.

items.question: How many doors provide access to the cabin, and what types, per Sect. 7.1.1?
options: Six doors: two hinged doors for front occupants, two sliding doors for rear passengers, two aft clamshell doors for the rear compartment
Four doors: two hinged front doors and two sliding rear doors only
Two doors total, one hinged and one sliding
Eight doors including two emergency exits
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1 states the cabin is accessible through six doors: two hinged doors for the front occupants, two sliding doors for the rear passengers, and two aft clamshell doors for the rear compartment.

items.question: How long can the two supply fuel tanks sustain flight in OEI condition, per Sect. 7.1.1?
options: Approximately 20 minutes, depending on level speed, pressure altitude, OAT, gross mass, torque, and installed optional equipment
Approximately 5 minutes fixed, regardless of conditions
Approximately 60 minutes fixed, regardless of conditions
The supply tanks provide no separate OEI endurance
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1 states the supply tanks provide sufficient separated fuel quantity for approximately 20 minutes of flight in OEI condition, depending on level speed, pressure altitude, OAT, gross mass, torque, and installed optional equipment.

items.question: What voltage does the electrical system supply when operated by the generators, versus when operated by the main battery, per Sect. 7.9.1?
options: About 28V DC via generators; about 24V DC via battery
About 24V DC via generators; about 28V DC via battery
115V AC via generators; 24V DC via battery
12V DC in both cases
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1 states that when operated by the generators, the electrical system supplies about 28V DC to the airborne electrical system, and about 24V DC when operated by the battery; the standby battery supplies about 24V DC to emergency equipment.

items.question: Which busbar connects consumers of secondary importance that are shed in case of a double generator failure, per Sect. 7.9.1?
options: SHED BUS 1 and 2
ESS BUS 1 and 2
HIGH LOAD BUS 1 and 2
EMER BUS
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1 describes the SHED BUSes 1 and 2 as connecting consumers of secondary importance that are shed in case of a double generator failure, each supplied by its PRIMARY BUS.

items.question: Which busbar supplies the standby air data and attitude indicator (IESI) and the emergency exit lights, per Sect. 7.9.1?
options: EMER BUS, supplied by ESS BUS 2 with an alternate supply from the standby battery
HIGH LOAD BUS 1, supplied only when both generators are running
PRIMARY BUS 1 only, with no alternate supply
BATTERY BUS directly, with no other bus involvement
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1 states the EMER BUS connects the standby air data and attitude indicator (IESI) and the emergency exit lights, supplied by ESS BUS 2 with an alternate power supply from the standby battery.

items.question: Which busbars connect all non-essential high load consumers, supplied only when both generators are running or an EPU is connected, per Sect. 7.9.1?
options: HIGH LOAD BUS 1 and 2
SHED BUS 1 and 2
EMER BUS
ESS BUS 1 and 2
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1 describes HIGH LOAD BUS 1 and 2 as connecting all non-essential high load consumers, which are supplied only when both generators are in operation or an EPU is connected.

items.question: How is a generator reset performed after it has been disconnected, per Sect. 7.9.2.1?
options: The GEN switch is momentarily set to the spring-loaded RES position, released to return to OFF, then set to NORM to reconnect
The generator resets automatically without pilot action
The battery master switch must be cycled OFF and ON
The GEN switch is held in RES position continuously for 30 seconds
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.2.1 describes the generator reset procedure: momentarily set the GEN switch to the spring-loaded RES position, release it to return to OFF, then set the switch to NORM to reconnect the generator.

items.question: What does the BAT MSTR switch control, per Sect. 7.9.2.2?
options: The battery system, the EPU system, and the essential contactors connecting the BAT BUS with ESS BUS 1 and ESS BUS 2
Only the standby battery, with no effect on the main battery or EPU
Only the generators, not the battery
The bleed air heating system exclusively
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.2.2 states the BAT MSTR switch controls the battery system, the EPU system, and the essential contactors connecting the BAT BUS with ESS BUS 1 and ESS BUS 2; when an EPU is connected, the BAT BUS is automatically disconnected from the PRIMARY BUSes.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.3, what color represents a disconnected or degraded generator (while its engine is running) on the electrical system display?
options: Amber
Green
Red
Light gray
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.3 gives the generator state symbol color logic: green = connected, amber = disconnected or degraded while its engine is running, light gray = off in normal conditions.

items.question: What color indicates battery overheat on the electrical system display, per Sect. 7.9.3?
options: Red
Amber
Green
Light gray
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.3 gives the battery state symbol color logic: green = connected, amber = disconnected or degraded, red = battery overheat, light gray = off with power provided by EPU.

items.question: On the electrical indication display, how is battery charging distinguished from battery discharging, per Sect. 7.9.3?
options: Charging is shown as negative current, discharging as positive current
Charging is shown as positive current, discharging as negative current
Both are shown identically; only the color differs
Charging and discharging cannot be distinguished on this display
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.3 states that battery charging is indicated as negative current, and discharging as positive current, on the digital indication.

items.question: Under what condition is the bleed air heating system automatically switched off, per Sect. 7.10.1?
options: Automatically by the FADEC or warning unit in case of OEI (N1 < 50%)
Automatically whenever the landing gear is extended
It is never automatically switched off; only manual control is provided
Automatically above 10,000 ft pressure altitude regardless of engine status
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.1 states the bleed air heating system is automatically switched off by the FADEC or the warning unit in case of OEI (N1 < 50%); depending on the power margin of the normal engine, it may be re-engaged via the BLD HTG EMER switch.

items.question: What triggers the HEATING OVERTEMP caution, per Sect. 7.10.1?
options: A malfunction of the heating mixing valve causing an air temperature increase above a specific threshold, detected by overtemperature switches in the cabin air duct
Any activation of the bleed air heating system regardless of temperature
Only a failure of the cockpit fan motor
Exceeding the maximum operating altitude
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.1 states that if a malfunction of the heating mixing valve causes an air temperature increase above a specific threshold value, one of the overtemperature switches (located in the cabin air duct) will cause the heating mixing valve to close and trigger the HEATING OVERTEMP caution.

items.question: When both engines return to N1 > 50%, what happens to the bleed air heating system, per Sect. 7.10.1?
options: It automatically returns to its normal function, switching on depending on the rheostat setting
It remains disabled until manually reset by maintenance
It must be manually re-armed via a circuit breaker before it will operate
It permanently stays in EMER mode until the next flight
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.1 states that when both engines are running (N1 > 50%), the bleed air heating will automatically return to its normal function, switching on depending on the rheostat setting.
